desc:
The strings s and t are anagrams: t is some rearrangement of the letters of s. Because letters can repeat, there are many ways to say which position of t each letter of s moved to, so use this canonical one: the k-th occurrence of a letter in s (counting from the left) is mapped to the k-th occurrence of the same letter in t.

Return the array m of length n where m[i] is the 0-based position in t that the letter s[i] is mapped to. For example, with s = "abca" and t = "caab" the answer is [1, 3, 0, 2]: the first a of s goes to the first a of t (index 1), b goes to index 3, c to index 0 and the second a to the second a of t (index 2).
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters
t is a rearrangement of s
hints: Searching t from scratch for every character of s costs O(n²). You only need to look at positions of one particular letter.
Collect, for every letter, the list of its positions in t in increasing order.
Walk through s from left to right with one pointer per letter: the letter c takes the next unused position from the list of c in t.
editorial: The canonical mapping pairs equal letters in order of appearance, so it is enough to know, for each letter, where it occurs in t. Build 26 lists of positions by scanning t once. Then scan s once; for the letter c keep a counter used[c] and answer pos[c][used[c]], then increase the counter.

This takes O(n) time and O(n) extra space. A mapping built by repeated searching (t.index after blanking out used characters) gives the same answer but is quadratic. Note that this particular mapping never makes two equal letters cross each other, which is exactly the property that makes it the cheapest way to turn s into t by adjacent swaps (see the related problem on adjacent swaps).
